why: ISO/IEC 27001 is the security certification clients, tenders and partners ask for most often in Europe, and SOC 2 is its counterpart with US clients. GRC analysts, ISMS coordinators and IT auditors are hired to run the management system, keep the evidence ready and get the company through audits without surprises.
outcome: explain what an ISMS is and what clauses 4 to 10 require, find your way in the 93 Annex A controls, write a Statement of Applicability, collect evidence that convinces an auditor, run an internal audit and handle nonconformities, prepare a certification audit, and explain how SOC 2 and other frameworks compare.

lessons.title: What an ISMS is and why companies certify
text: An information security management system (ISMS) is the way a company organises itself to protect its information: who decides, how risks are assessed, which controls are chosen, how they are checked and improved. It is not a tool or a firewall. It is a management system, like ISO 9001 for quality: policies, roles, processes and records that run in a cycle of plan, do, check, act.

ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard that sets the requirements for an ISMS. The current edition is ISO/IEC 27001:2022, published in October 2022; Amendment 1 of 2024 added that the organisation must consider whether climate change is a relevant issue when it determines its context. Certificates to the old 2013 edition had to move to the 2022 edition within a three-year transition that ended in October 2025. Its companion ISO/IEC 27002:2022 is not certifiable: it gives guidance on how to implement each control listed in Annex A of 27001.

Companies certify mainly because clients ask. A SaaS vendor answering a bank’s security questionnaire, a supplier bidding in a public tender, a hosting provider: a valid certificate answers dozens of questions at once and shortens the sales cycle. Certification also gives management a yearly rhythm of risk review, internal audit and improvement, and an outside view from an independent auditor.

A certificate covers a scope, not the whole company by default. “ISMS supporting the development and operation of the X platform, Paris and Tunis offices” is a typical scope statement. Reading the scope on a supplier’s certificate is the first thing a GRC analyst does: a certificate that covers only the head office says nothing about the data centre that hosts your data.

In a GRC team, the ISMS is daily work: keeping the risk register and the Statement of Applicability up to date, chasing evidence from IT and HR, running awareness campaigns, preparing internal audits and the management review, and answering client questionnaires with the certificate and its scope.
points: ISMS = management system for information security: policies, roles, risk process, controls, review.
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 sets requirements and is certifiable; ISO/IEC 27002:2022 gives implementation guidance and is not.
The certificate is only as useful as its scope: always read the scope statement.
Plan, do, check, act: the ISMS is a cycle, not a one-off project.

example.code:
Certificate check on a supplier (vendor review)
  Standard:        ISO/IEC 27001:2022            OK (not the 2013 edition)
  Scope:           "Development and hosting of the Payroll SaaS, Lyon office and AWS eu-west-3"
  Our use:         Payroll SaaS                  covered
  Valid until:     2027-03-14                    OK
  Issued by:       accredited certification body  check the accreditation mark
  SoA version:     v4, 2025-11-02                ask for it if controls matter to us
example.note: Five checks on a supplier certificate: edition, scope, validity, issuer accreditation and the Statement of Applicability version.

lessons.title: Clauses 4 to 10 in practice
text: The requirements of ISO/IEC 27001 are in clauses 4 to 10 (clauses 1 to 3 are scope, references and terms). They follow the harmonised structure shared by ISO management system standards: 4 Context of the organisation, 5 Leadership, 6 Planning, 7 Support, 8 Operation, 9 Performance evaluation, 10 Improvement. An organisation cannot exclude any of these clauses: all of them are mandatory to be certified.

Clause 4 asks you to understand the context (internal and external issues), the interested parties and their requirements (clients, regulators, staff), and to define the scope of the ISMS with its interfaces and dependencies. Clause 5 puts top management on the hook: an information security policy, roles and responsibilities assigned, resources provided. Auditors interview management to check that this is real and not delegated to one engineer.

Clause 6 is the core. 6.1.2 requires a defined risk assessment process: criteria for acceptance, identification of risks to confidentiality, integrity and availability, risk owners, analysis and evaluation that give consistent, comparable results. 6.1.3 requires risk treatment: choose options (modify, retain, avoid, share), determine the necessary controls, compare them with Annex A, produce the Statement of Applicability and a risk treatment plan approved by the risk owners. 6.2 sets measurable security objectives, and 6.3, new in 2022, asks that changes to the ISMS be planned.

Clause 7 covers support: resources, competence, awareness, communication and documented information (7.5), meaning documents and records that are created, approved, versioned and controlled. Clause 8 is operation: carry out the plans, perform risk assessments at planned intervals or after significant changes, and implement the risk treatment plan. Clause 9 is performance evaluation: monitoring and measurement (9.1), internal audit (9.2) and management review (9.3). Clause 10 is improvement: continual improvement (10.1) and nonconformity and corrective action (10.2).

In practice, an auditor walks through these clauses with a list of documented information the standard requires, such as the scope, the policy, the risk assessment and treatment processes and results, the Statement of Applicability, objectives, evidence of competence, monitoring results, the audit programme and results, management review results, and nonconformities with their corrective actions.
points: 4 Context, 5 Leadership, 6 Planning, 7 Support, 8 Operation, 9 Performance evaluation, 10 Improvement.
Clauses 4 to 10 cannot be excluded; only Annex A controls can be excluded, with a justification.
6.1.2 risk assessment and 6.1.3 risk treatment produce the Statement of Applicability and the risk treatment plan.
Documented information (7.5) must be controlled: owner, version, approval, review date.

example.code:
Clause  What the auditor asks for                       Typical evidence
4.3     Scope of the ISMS                                Scope document, approved and dated
5.2     Information security policy                      Signed policy, published on the intranet
6.1.2   Risk assessment process and results              Method + risk register with owners
6.1.3   Risk treatment and Statement of Applicability    SoA v4 + treatment plan signed by risk owners
7.2     Competence                                       Training records, CVs for key roles
9.2     Internal audit                                   Audit programme, reports, auditor independence
9.3     Management review                                Minutes with inputs, decisions and actions
10.2    Nonconformity and corrective action              NC log with root cause and closure evidence
example.note: A clause-by-clause evidence list like this is the backbone of audit preparation.

lessons.title: Annex A: the four themes and examples
text: Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 lists 93 reference controls, grouped in four themes: organizational controls (37, numbered 5.1 to 5.37), people controls (8, numbered 6.1 to 6.8), physical controls (14, numbered 7.1 to 7.14) and technological controls (34, numbered 8.1 to 8.34). The numbering starts at 5 because it mirrors the chapters of ISO/IEC 27002:2022, where chapters 5 to 8 describe the same controls with guidance.

The 2013 edition had 114 controls in 14 domains. The 2022 revision merged many of them and added 11 new controls, among them threat intelligence (5.7), information security for use of cloud services (5.23), ICT readiness for business continuity (5.30), physical security monitoring (7.4), configuration management (8.9), information deletion (8.10), data masking (8.11), data leakage prevention (8.12), monitoring activities (8.16), web filtering (8.23) and secure coding (8.28). Interviewers like asking about these because they show whether you know the current edition.

Organizational controls are the largest theme: policies (5.1), roles and segregation of duties (5.2, 5.3), asset inventory (5.9), access control and access rights (5.15, 5.18), supplier security (5.19 to 5.22), incident management (5.24 to 5.28), business continuity, legal and privacy requirements. People controls cover the employee lifecycle: screening (6.1), terms of employment (6.2), awareness and training (6.3), the disciplinary process (6.4), responsibilities after leaving (6.5), confidentiality agreements (6.6), remote working (6.7) and event reporting (6.8).

Physical controls protect places and equipment: perimeters and entry (7.1, 7.2), securing offices (7.3), clear desk and clear screen (7.7), storage media (7.10), supporting utilities (7.11) and secure disposal or reuse of equipment (7.14). Technological controls are what IT runs: user endpoint devices (8.1), privileged access rights (8.2), secure authentication (8.5), protection against malware (8.7), management of technical vulnerabilities (8.8), backup (8.13), logging (8.15), network security (8.20), use of cryptography (8.24) and change management (8.32).

ISO/IEC 27002:2022 also gives each control five attributes (control type, information security properties, cybersecurity concepts, operational capabilities, security domains). They let you filter the catalogue, for example to list every preventive control, or every control that maps to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework function Detect.
points: 93 controls: organizational 37, people 8, physical 14, technological 34.
Numbering 5.x to 8.x mirrors the chapters of ISO/IEC 27002:2022.
11 controls are new in 2022, such as threat intelligence, cloud services, data masking, data leakage prevention and secure coding.
Annex A is a reference list to compare your controls with, not a mandatory checklist.

example.code:
Theme            Count  Numbers      Examples
Organizational   37     5.1-5.37     5.1 Policies, 5.15 Access control, 5.19 Supplier relationships, 5.24 Incident management planning
People            8     6.1-6.8      6.1 Screening, 6.3 Awareness and training, 6.7 Remote working
Physical         14     7.1-7.14     7.2 Physical entry, 7.7 Clear desk and clear screen, 7.14 Secure disposal
Technological    34     8.1-8.34     8.2 Privileged access rights, 8.8 Technical vulnerabilities, 8.13 Backup, 8.32 Change management
Total            93
example.note: 37 + 8 + 14 + 34 = 93: worth knowing by heart for interviews.

lessons.title: The Statement of Applicability
text: The Statement of Applicability (SoA) is the document that links your risks to your controls. Clause 6.1.3 d) requires it to contain the necessary controls, the justification for including them, whether they are implemented or not, and the justification for excluding any Annex A control. In practice it is a table with one line per Annex A control, plus any extra controls you added yourself.

A control is included because the risk assessment needs it, because a law or contract requires it, or because it is part of a client commitment. The justification must say which: “Included: risks R-07 and R-12 (unauthorised access to client data), client contracts require quarterly access reviews.” An exclusion must be just as explicit: “Excluded 7.5 Protecting against physical and environmental threats for the data centre: no data centre in scope, hosting on AWS eu-west-3; supplier risk covered by 5.19 to 5.23.”

Auditors read the SoA against the risk treatment plan. A control marked “not applicable” while the risk register lists a risk it would treat is a finding. So is a control marked “implemented” with no evidence behind it, or an exclusion justified by “not relevant” without a reason. Many companies exclude very few controls; excluding is legitimate, but only when the justification would convince a sceptical reader.

Keep the SoA alive: a version number, an owner, an approval by management, a review at least yearly and after significant changes (new office, new cloud provider, new product in scope). Clients sometimes ask for it in due diligence: it shows the real coverage of a certificate far better than the certificate alone.

A useful SoA has more columns than the standard requires: the control owner, the implementation status (implemented, partly, planned with a date), the reference to the policy or procedure, and where the evidence lives. That turns it into the map the GRC analyst uses to prepare every audit.
points: The SoA lists necessary controls, why each is included, whether it is implemented, and why any Annex A control is excluded.
Justify inclusions by risks, legal or contractual requirements; justify exclusions with facts about the scope.
The SoA must be consistent with the risk treatment plan and the risk register.
Version it, approve it, review it at least yearly and after significant changes.

example.code:
Control                                   Applicable  Justification                                              Status        Owner     Evidence
5.15 Access control                       Yes         Risks R-07, R-12; client contracts (access reviews)          Implemented   IT Ops    Access policy v3, quarterly review exports
8.11 Data masking                         Yes         Risk R-15: production data copied to test environments      Planned Q2    Dev lead  Treatment plan item T-09
7.11 Supporting utilities                 No          No server room in scope; hosting on AWS eu-west-3,           -             -         Supplier review of AWS under 5.22
                                                      covered by supplier controls 5.19-5.23
example.note: Each line answers: is it needed, why, is it done, who owns it, where is the proof.

lessons.title: Evidence and control testing
text: Auditors test controls in two steps. Design effectiveness: is the control, as described, able to prevent or detect the risk (right frequency, right people, right scope)? Operating effectiveness: did it actually work as designed throughout the period? A beautiful access review procedure is well designed; three quarters of signed review exports show it operates.

They use four kinds of procedures, from weakest to strongest: inquiry (asking someone), observation (watching the control being performed), inspection (examining documents, records, configurations) and reperformance (doing the control again to see if the result is the same). Inquiry alone is never enough. A walkthrough follows one transaction from start to end to confirm the design.

For a control that runs many times, the auditor tests a sample. The population must be complete and come from the system itself (for example all change tickets of the period exported from the tool, with the query used), and the sample must be chosen by the auditor, not the auditee. A common rule of thumb in audit firms is to scale the sample with the control frequency: 1 for an annual control, 2 for quarterly, 2 to 5 for monthly, 5 to 15 for weekly and 20 to 40 for daily or more frequent controls. Each firm has its own table.

Good evidence is relevant (it shows the control, not something nearby), reliable (system-generated, hard to alter), dated within the audit period, complete (the full population, the parameters of the report) and traceable to who did what and when. A screenshot without date or source, an e-mail saying “all good”, or a procedure that nobody signed are weak evidence. A deviation (exception) found in a sample is analysed: isolated error, or a sign that the control does not work?

GRC teams prepare a PBC list (“provided by client”): every piece of evidence the auditor will ask for, its owner and its due date. Collecting evidence continuously during the year, rather than the week before the audit, is the difference between a calm audit and a crisis.
points: Design effectiveness = the control can work; operating effectiveness = it did work over the period.
Inquiry < observation < inspection < reperformance; inquiry alone never proves a control.
Sample from a complete, system-generated population; the auditor picks the sample.
Good evidence is relevant, reliable, dated, complete and traceable.

example.code:
A: Control                  B: Frequency  C: Sample  D: Exceptions
Quarterly access review       Quarterly     2          0
Change approval               Daily         25         1
Backup restore test           Monthly       2          0

E2: exception rate of the change sample
=D3/C3        -> 0.04  (1 of 25 changes had no approval)
example.note: One exception in 25 is a 4 % rate: the auditor asks why, checks whether it is isolated, and may extend the sample.

lessons.title: Internal audit, nonconformities and management review
text: Clause 9.2 requires internal audits at planned intervals to check that the ISMS conforms to the organisation’s own requirements and to ISO/IEC 27001, and that it is effectively implemented and maintained. You need an audit programme (frequency, methods, responsibilities, reporting), criteria and scope for each audit, and auditors chosen to be objective and impartial: nobody audits their own work. ISO 19011 gives guidelines for auditing management systems.

A typical programme covers every clause and all applicable Annex A controls over the three-year certification cycle, with high-risk areas audited every year. Each audit has a plan, an opening meeting, interviews and evidence review, and a closing meeting where findings are presented, then a written report.

A nonconformity is the non-fulfilment of a requirement (of the standard, of your own policy, of a contract or law). Certification bodies grade them: a major nonconformity is the absence or total breakdown of a requirement, or a failure that raises serious doubt about the ISMS achieving its outcomes (no internal audit at all, no risk assessment, access reviews never performed). A minor nonconformity is an isolated lapse that does not call the system into question (one leaver’s account disabled late out of forty). An observation or opportunity for improvement is not a nonconformity.

Clause 10.2 sets what to do: react to the nonconformity (control and correct it, deal with the consequences), find the root cause, check whether similar nonconformities exist or could occur, implement corrective action, review its effectiveness and update the ISMS if needed. A correction fixes the case (disable the account); a corrective action removes the cause (automate the HR-to-IT leaver feed). Auditors want both, with evidence.

Clause 9.3 management review closes the loop: top management reviews at planned intervals the status of past actions, changes in context, feedback on performance (nonconformities, monitoring results, audit results, security objectives), interested parties’ feedback, risk assessment results and opportunities for improvement. The minutes must show decisions and actions, not only a slide deck presented.
points: Internal audits: a programme, objective and impartial auditors, reports to management (9.2).
Major NC = requirement absent or system breakdown; minor NC = isolated lapse; observation = not a nonconformity.
Correction fixes the case; corrective action removes the root cause (10.2).
Management review (9.3) records decisions and actions from defined inputs.

example.code:
NC-2026-04  Minor   Clause 9.2 / Annex A 5.18
Finding:     Q2 access review for the CRM not performed (Q1, Q3 done).
Correction:  Q2 review run late on 2026-09-02; 3 obsolete accounts removed.
Root cause:  Review owner left in May; task not reassigned.
Corrective:  Reviews scheduled in the GRC tool with a named owner and a deputy;
             overdue alerts to the CISO.
Effectiveness check: Q4 review done on time -> closed 2027-01-10.
example.note: Finding, correction, root cause, corrective action and an effectiveness check: the full 10.2 cycle.

lessons.title: The certification audit
text: Certification is done by a certification body, ideally accredited for ISO/IEC 27001 by a national accreditation body: COFRAC in France, UKAS in the United Kingdom, DAkkS in Germany, all members of the International Accreditation Forum. Certification bodies follow ISO/IEC 17021-1 and the ISMS-specific ISO/IEC 27006. A certificate from a non-accredited body may be refused by clients and in tenders: check the accreditation before signing.

The initial audit has two stages. Stage 1 reviews the documentation and readiness: scope, policy, risk assessment, SoA, internal audit and management review done, and plans stage 2. Stage 2, usually a few weeks later, evaluates implementation and effectiveness on site or remotely: interviews, sampling of evidence, controls in operation. Findings from stage 1 must be addressed before stage 2.

After stage 2, major nonconformities must be corrected, with evidence accepted by the auditor, before certification can be granted; minor nonconformities need an accepted corrective action plan, checked at the next audit. The auditor recommends; the certification body’s independent decision-maker grants the certificate.

A certificate is valid for three years. Surveillance audits take place at least once a year in years one and two, on a sample of clauses and controls plus the follow-up of past findings. A recertification audit before expiry starts a new three-year cycle. Significant changes (new site, scope extension) are reported to the certification body and may trigger an extra audit.

Typical preparation: a gap analysis against the standard, the risk assessment and SoA, controls implemented and running for some months to have records, one full internal audit and a management review before stage 1. Audit days depend on the number of people in scope and complexity (ISO/IEC 27006 gives the method). During the audit, the GRC analyst organises interviews, provides evidence quickly, and never hides a problem: a known issue with a corrective plan is far better than one the auditor discovers.
points: Stage 1 = documentation and readiness; stage 2 = implementation and effectiveness.
Major NCs closed before certification; minor NCs need an accepted action plan.
Three-year cycle: certification, surveillance in years 1 and 2, recertification.
Choose an accredited certification body (COFRAC in France, UKAS in the UK).

example.code:
Year 0   Gap analysis -> risk assessment, SoA -> controls running -> internal audit -> management review
         Stage 1 (documentation, readiness)
         Stage 2 (implementation, effectiveness) -> NCs closed -> certificate issued (valid 3 years)
Year 1   Surveillance audit 1
Year 2   Surveillance audit 2
Year 3   Recertification audit before expiry -> new 3-year certificate
example.note: The cycle repeats; every audit also follows up the findings of the previous one.

lessons.title: SOC 2 and other frameworks compared
text: SOC 2 is an attestation report, not a certification. It is defined by the AICPA (American Institute of Certified Public Accountants) and issued by a licensed CPA firm under its attestation standards. The report covers the Trust Services Criteria: security (always in scope, the “common criteria”), and optionally availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. The company describes its system and its controls; the auditor gives an opinion on them.

A Type I report gives an opinion on the design of the controls at a point in time (“as of 30 June”). A Type II report covers the design and the operating effectiveness of the controls over a period, usually six to twelve months, with tests and any exceptions listed. Clients usually want a Type II; a Type I is often a first step for a young company. SOC 1 is about controls relevant to clients’ financial reporting; SOC 3 is a short general-use version of SOC 2.

Which one when? European clients, public tenders and many industries ask for ISO/IEC 27001 certification. North American clients, especially for SaaS, ask for a SOC 2 Type II report. Payment card data brings PCI DSS; in France, health data hosting needs HDS certification (built on ISO/IEC 27001), and some public sector cloud needs ANSSI’s SecNumCloud qualification. ISO/IEC 27701 extends an ISMS to privacy; the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) is a voluntary framework widely used to structure a programme.

Most of the work is shared. An access review, a change management process, backups tested, vendor reviews, incident response: the same control satisfies ISO 27001 Annex A, the SOC 2 common criteria and PCI DSS requirements. Mature GRC teams keep one control library, map each control once to every framework (“test once, comply many”), collect evidence once and reuse it in each audit. GRC tools (ServiceNow GRC, OneTrust, Vanta, Drata and others) are built around this mapping.

The differences matter too. ISO 27001 certifies a management system (risk process, SoA, internal audit, management review) and the certificate is public; SOC 2 reports on controls against criteria, for a period, and the report is restricted to clients under NDA. A SOC 2 report lists exceptions in detail; an ISO certificate does not list nonconformities. Explain this clearly when a client asks “are you SOC 2 or ISO?”.
points: SOC 2 = AICPA attestation by a CPA firm on the Trust Services Criteria; security is always included.
Type I = design at a point in time; Type II = design and operating effectiveness over a period.
ISO 27001 certifies a management system; SOC 2 reports on controls; both are often needed.
Map controls once to many frameworks and reuse evidence (“test once, comply many”).

example.code:
Control C-12  Quarterly user access review (owner: IT Ops)
  ISO/IEC 27001:2022   Annex A 5.15 Access control, 5.18 Access rights
  SOC 2 (TSC 2017)     CC6.1, CC6.2, CC6.3 (logical access)
  PCI DSS v4.0         Requirement 7 (restrict access by business need to know)
  Evidence             Review export per system, signed by the manager, removals ticketed
  Tested               Internal audit Q3; SOC 2 Type II sample; ISO surveillance audit
example.note: One control, one evidence pack, three frameworks: the core of an efficient compliance programme.

lessons.title: ITGC and IT audit in a financial statement audit
text: Accounts are produced by systems: an ERP such as SAP, Oracle, Sage or Cegid, a payroll tool, a billing application and the interfaces between them. The statutory auditors (commissaires aux comptes in France) must understand this IT environment and the risks that come from it: the international standard ISA 315 and the French professional standards (NEP) require it. When the audit team relies on an automated control (a three-way match that blocks an invoice) or on a system report (an aged receivables list), it needs assurance that the system behaved the same way all year and that nobody could change programs or data without control. That assurance comes from the IT general controls (ITGC). In audit firms, including the Big 4, IT auditors (“IT audit”, “technology risk” or “digital assurance” teams) test them for the financial audit team; internal audit and SOX teams in large groups do the same work.

ITGC are usually grouped in four domains. Access to programs and data: user creation approved, leavers removed on time, periodic access reviews, password and authentication settings, privileged accounts restricted and monitored. Program changes: each change to production is requested, tested, approved, and deployed by someone other than its developer. Program development: new systems and major projects (an ERP migration) are tested, data migration is reconciled and go-live is approved. Computer operations: batch jobs and interfaces are monitored and failures resolved, backups run and are restored in tests, incidents are handled. Some firms merge development into change management and present three domains; the content is the same.

ITGC support the application controls, which sit inside the business process: an automated credit limit check, a payment that needs two approvers above a threshold, a calculation of depreciation, a field that cannot be left empty. Because a program does the same thing every time, a common practice is to test an automated control with one example per scenario (“test of one”), provided the program-change ITGC are effective over the period. Reports deserve the same care: the auditors test the completeness and accuracy of every information produced by the entity (IPE) that a control or a test relies on, checking the report’s logic or parameters and reconciling it to a known total. Segregation of duties (SoD) and privileged access run through all of this: the same person should not create a vendor and approve its payment, or develop a change and push it to production; administrator accounts (SAP_ALL, database administrators, emergency “firefighter” accounts) are few, named and their use is logged and reviewed.

SOX section 404, in one paragraph: the US Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires the management of companies listed in the US to assess their internal control over financial reporting each year (404(a)) and, for larger filers, the external auditor to give an opinion on it (404(b)). French subsidiaries of US-listed groups, and French groups listed in the US, test their key controls, ITGC included, on the group’s calendar. Whatever the framework, testing has two steps. The test of design checks that the control, as described, would prevent or detect the risk: inquiry, reading the procedure and a walkthrough of one transaction. The test of operating effectiveness checks that it worked all period: inspection of records, observation and reperformance on a sample. Inquiry alone is never enough evidence.

Sampling starts from a complete population taken from the system (all production changes of the year, all leavers from the HR file), with evidence of how it was extracted; the auditor, not the auditee, picks the sample. Sample sizes depend on the control’s frequency, and each firm sets its own table; a common practice is 1 for an annual control, 2 for a quarterly one, 2 to 5 for monthly, 5 to 15 for weekly, 20 to 40 for daily, and more for controls that run many times a day. An exception (a sampled change with no approval) is first investigated: cause, isolated or not, other items affected, compensating controls. Depending on the firm’s method, the sample may be extended or the control concluded ineffective. A deficiency is then rated for severity: control deficiency, significant deficiency or, under SOX, material weakness. The statutory auditors communicate significant deficiencies to management and governance (ISA 265, NEP 265), and give recommendations in a management letter; the audit team adapts its approach, for example with more substantive testing when it can no longer rely on a system.
points: ITGC domains: access to programs and data, program changes, program development, computer operations.
ITGC let auditors rely on automated application controls and system reports (IPE) all year.
Test of design = would it work (inquiry, walkthrough); operating effectiveness = did it work all period (sample).
Sample sizes by frequency come from each firm’s methodology; the population must be complete and system-generated.
Exception → investigate cause and extent → rate the deficiency → report it and adapt the audit approach.

example.code:
ITGC test  PC-02  Changes to production are approved before deployment (SAP FI)
  Population   Transport log, 1 Jan - 31 Dec: 212 changes (extracted by IT, query and totals kept)
  Frequency    Ad hoc, 212 occurrences  ->  sample of 25 (firm table by population size), picked by the auditor
  Attributes   A ticket exists | business approval dated before import | tested in QA | developer != deployer
  Results      24 OK, 1 exception: CHG-2045 imported by an admin account, no approval
  Follow-up    Cause: emergency fix, approval never recorded; admin account shared by two people
               Compensating control? Monthly change log review by the finance controller: not performed in June
  Conclusion   Deficiency, PC-02 not effective; impact on automated controls and IPE assessed with the audit team
  Reported     Management letter recommendation; discussed with the CFO and the CIO
example.note: One control, its population, its sample and one exception followed to a conclusion: the shape of an ITGC workpaper.

items: Information security management system: policies, roles, risk process, controls, review
Certifiable standard with the ISMS requirements (clauses 4 to 10 + Annex A)
Guidance on implementing each Annex A control; not certifiable
Issues, interested parties, scope of the ISMS
Continual improvement, nonconformity and corrective action (10.2)
37 controls, 5.1 to 5.37 (policies, access control, suppliers, incidents)
11 controls such as threat intelligence, data masking, secure coding
Necessary controls, justification, implemented or not, justified exclusions
Actions chosen to treat risks, approved by the risk owners
Risk, legal or contractual requirement behind a control
Fact about the scope that makes an Annex A control unnecessary
Person accountable for a risk and for accepting the residual risk
The control, as designed, can prevent or detect the risk
The control worked as designed over the whole period
The auditor redoes the control to check the result
Following one transaction end to end to confirm the design
Complete, system-generated list of occurrences a sample is drawn from
Provided by client: evidence requested, owner, due date
A sample item where the control did not work
Requirement absent or total breakdown; must be closed before certification
Isolated lapse; accepted corrective action plan
Removes the root cause so it does not recur
Top management reviews ISMS performance and decides actions (9.3)
Yearly audit in years 1 and 2 of the 3-year cycle
French accreditation body for certification bodies
AICPA attestation report by a CPA firm on the Trust Services Criteria
Security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy
Design of controls at a point in time
Design and operating effectiveness over a period
One control library mapped to every framework
IT general controls: access, program changes, program development, computer operations
Automated or IT-dependent control inside a business process (credit limit, three-way match)
Information produced by the entity: a report whose completeness and accuracy are tested
Incompatible tasks (create vendor and approve payment) held by different people
US rule: management assesses internal control over financial reporting; larger filers get an auditor opinion
SOX: deficiency (or combination) with a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement is not prevented or detected in time

pitfalls: Reading a supplier’s ISO 27001 certificate without checking its scope: it may not cover the service you buy.
Excluding Annex A controls with “not relevant” and no reason, or marking controls implemented with no evidence behind them.
An SoA that does not match the risk register and the risk treatment plan.
Collecting evidence the week before the audit: missing quarters cannot be recreated afterwards.
Accepting screenshots without date or source, or letting the auditee choose the sample.
Fixing the case (correction) without removing the root cause (corrective action), so the same finding returns.
Telling a US client “we are ISO certified, so we have SOC 2”: they are different reports for different audiences.
Testing a control with a system report or a population without checking its completeness and accuracy (IPE): every conclusion then rests on a list nobody checked.

exercises.q: Match each ISO/IEC 27001 clause with its main topic.
pairs: Planning: risk assessment, risk treatment, objectives
Support: resources, competence, awareness, documented information
Operation: carrying out the risk treatment plan
Performance evaluation: monitoring, internal audit, management review
exercises.answer: Clauses 4 to 10 follow the harmonised structure of ISO management system standards. All are mandatory: only Annex A controls can be excluded.

exercises.q: Sort these Annex A controls into their 2022 theme.

groups.name: Physical
items: Secure disposal or re-use of equipment

exercises.q: How many controls does Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 list?
exercises.answer: 93 controls in four themes: organizational 37, people 8, physical 14, technological 34. The 2013 edition had 114.

exercises.q: Put the steps of an ISO/IEC 27001 certification cycle in order.
steps: Gap analysis, risk assessment and Statement of Applicability
Recertification audit before the certificate expires
exercises.answer: The organisation needs records of a running ISMS, including one internal audit and a management review, before stage 1. The certificate lasts three years with yearly surveillance.

exercises.q: A client asks for “a SOC 2 report that shows your controls worked over the last year”. What do they want?
exercises.answer: Type II covers the design and the operating effectiveness of controls over a period (usually 6 to 12 months). Type I only covers design at a point in time; SOC 1 is about financial reporting controls.

exercises.q: During stage 2, the auditor finds that no internal audit has ever been carried out. How is this usually graded?
exercises.answer: A required process (clause 9.2) is completely absent: a major nonconformity. It must be corrected, with evidence, before the certificate can be issued. One late audit report would be a minor.

exercises.q: Which evidence best proves that the quarterly access review operated during the audit period?
options: The IT manager confirms in the interview that reviews are always done
The access review procedure, approved by the CISO
For each quarter, the system export of accounts reviewed, signed and dated by the manager, with the removal tickets
An undated screenshot of the user list
exercises.answer: Operating effectiveness needs dated, complete, traceable records for each occurrence. Inquiry alone is never enough, a procedure only shows design, and an undated screenshot is not reliable.

exercises.q: In H2, count the Annex A controls of the theme typed in G2 that are applicable (Yes) and implemented.
exercises.hint: COUNTIFS takes range / condition pairs; point at G2 for the theme.
exercises.explain: COUNTIFS(B2:B9,G2,C2:C9,"Yes",D2:D9,"Implemented") gives 2 for Technological (8.2 and 8.13). Change G2 to Organizational and it gives 1. The same formula, one line per theme, builds the SoA status table for management.

exercises.q: In F2, the share of applicable controls that are implemented (a ratio between 0 and 1).
exercises.hint: Divide the total implemented by the total applicable, not by the 93 controls.
exercises.explain: SUM(D2:D5)/SUM(C2:C5) = 72 / 85 = 0.847, about 85 %. Dividing by the 93 controls (77 %) would penalise justified exclusions. Format the cell as a percentage.

exercises.q: In F2, the sample size for the control frequency typed in E2, read from the firm’s sampling table.
exercises.hint: XLOOKUP(what, where to look, what to return), or INDEX with MATCH.
exercises.explain: XLOOKUP(E2,A2:A7,B2:B7) returns 5 for a weekly control. INDEX(B2:B7,MATCH(E2,A2:A7,0)) works too. Keep the table in one place so every tester uses the same sizes.

exercises.q: In the stage 2 audit, the auditor asks for evidence of the quarterly access reviews for the last two quarters. You find none for the HR system. What do you do?

steps.text: The auditor is waiting for the evidence. First move?

choices.label: Tell the auditor openly that the HR system reviews were not performed and that you are investigating
choices.feedback: Transparency keeps your credibility; the auditor will find it anyway in the sample.

choices.label: Run the review today and present it as the Q2 review
choices.feedback: Backdating evidence is falsification: it can cost the certificate and your job.

choices.label: Say the HR system is out of scope
choices.feedback: If the scope and SoA include it, this contradicts your own documents and damages trust.

steps.text: The auditor raises a nonconformity on control 5.18 Access rights. What do you put in the response?

choices.label: Correction (review run now, dated today, obsolete accounts removed), root cause, corrective action and how you will check it works
choices.feedback: That is the full clause 10.2 response the auditor expects.

choices.label: Only the correction: the review has now been done
choices.feedback: Without a root cause and corrective action, the same gap will come back next quarter.

steps.text: The root cause: the review owner left and nobody took over. Best corrective action?

choices.label: Schedule reviews in the GRC tool with a named owner and deputy, overdue alerts to the CISO, and check the next quarter
choices.feedback: It removes the cause (single point of failure) and includes an effectiveness check.

choices.label: Send a reminder e-mail to IT about access reviews
choices.feedback: A reminder does not remove the cause and leaves no follow-up.

exercises.answer: Be transparent, never backdate evidence. Respond with correction, root cause, corrective action and an effectiveness check, and keep the evidence of each step for the next audit.

exercises.q: Draft three lines of a Statement of Applicability for a 60-person SaaS company hosted fully on a public cloud (no server room, one office): 5.23 Information security for use of cloud services, 7.11 Supporting utilities, and 8.11 Data masking. For each: applicable or not, justification, status.
exercises.answer: 5.23 Information security for use of cloud services: applicable. Justification: all production runs on the cloud provider (risks R-03 misconfiguration, R-05 provider outage); client contracts require it. Status: implemented (cloud security policy v2, shared responsibility matrix, configuration baseline checked monthly). 7.11 Supporting utilities: not applicable for servers. Justification: no server room or data centre in scope; the provider’s utilities are covered by supplier controls 5.19 to 5.23 and its own certification, reviewed yearly. The office has no equipment critical to the service (laptops only). Status: N/A. 8.11 Data masking: applicable. Justification: risk R-15, production data copied into test environments; GDPR obligations on personal data. Status: planned, masking scripts in the treatment plan item T-09 for Q2, owner the development lead. Each line names the risk or requirement, a concrete status and an owner, consistent with the risk treatment plan.

exercises.q: Access review on SAP FI. In G2, count the accounts still Active whose user has an HR leave date (leavers still active).
exercises.hint: Two conditions: status Active, and a leave date that is not empty ("<>").
exercises.explain: COUNTIFS(C2:C11,"Active",D2:D11,"<>") gives 3: u102, u105 and u108. "<>" alone means “not empty”. u102 and u108 even logged in after their leave date: those two are the exceptions to raise first, because the access was used. In practice the HR leavers list and the system user list are two extracts joined on an employee ID (XLOOKUP) before this count.

exercises.q: Change management test. In H2, count the changes to Production for the application typed in G2 that have no approver.
exercises.hint: Three conditions: the application in G2, the Production environment, and an empty approver ("").
exercises.explain: COUNTIFS(B2:B11,G2,C2:C11,"Production",D2:D11,"") gives 3 for SAP FI (CHG-2042, 2045, 2049) and 2 for Billing. Changes in Test are out of the control’s scope. "" as a criterion counts empty cells. Each one is an exception to investigate: an emergency change approved afterwards is handled differently from a change nobody ever approved.

exercises.q: Segregation of duties in purchasing. In F2, count the users who hold both Create vendor and Approve payment.
exercises.hint: One COUNTIFS with two range / condition pairs, both "Yes".
exercises.explain: COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"Yes",C2:C9,"Yes") gives 3: ap.clerk2, fin.manager and it.support. Creating a vendor and paying it is the classic fraud path (a fictitious supplier). An IT support account with business roles is a finding on its own. Each conflict is either removed or kept with a documented, tested mitigating control (for example a monthly review of new vendors paid).

exercises.q: Match each area with a control that belongs to it.
pairs: Leavers’ accounts are disabled within an agreed time after HR records the departure
Each change is tested and approved before it is moved to production
Data migrated to the new ERP is reconciled and the go-live is signed off
Failed batch jobs and interfaces are tracked and resolved; backups are restored in tests
The ERP blocks a payment above the threshold until a second person approves it
exercises.answer: The first four are the ITGC domains; the last is an application control inside the purchase-to-pay process, which the auditors can rely on only if the ITGC around it are effective.

exercises.q: Sort this evidence: does it support the test of design or the test of operating effectiveness?

groups.name: Test of design
items: Walkthrough of one change from request to deployment
Reading the change procedure and the approval matrix
Interview of the control owner on how the review is done

groups.name: Test of operating effectiveness
items: Approvals inspected for 25 changes sampled from the system’s change list
Reperformance of the access review for 2 sampled quarters
For each sampled leaver, disable date compared with the HR leave date

exercises.answer: Design is about whether the control, as described, can catch the risk: inquiry, documents, one walkthrough. Operating effectiveness needs evidence for a sample over the whole period: inspection and reperformance. An interview supports design but never proves operation on its own.

exercises.q: You test the SAP FI change control: 25 changes sampled from the year’s transport log. One change was imported by an administrator account with no approval. What do you do?

steps.text: You have just found the exception. First move?

choices.label: Ask the control owner for any approval or explanation, and look at the change itself and the account that imported it
choices.feedback: Confirm the facts first: an emergency change approved by e-mail afterwards is not the same as an unauthorised change.

choices.label: Ignore it: 24 out of 25 is good enough
choices.feedback: An exception is never dropped silently; it must be investigated and documented.

choices.label: Write straight away that the change control has a material weakness
choices.feedback: Severity is assessed after investigation and with the audit team, not on one item.

steps.text: No approval exists. The admin account is shared by two IT engineers and can import changes directly. Next?

choices.label: Assess the extent: other changes made with that account, what the change touched, and whether a compensating control (a monitored change log review) worked
choices.feedback: Root cause and extent decide whether the exception is isolated and how far reliance on the system is affected.

choices.label: Ask IT to approve the change today so the sample is clean
choices.feedback: Evidence created after the fact is not evidence that the control operated; it would mislead the audit.

steps.text: The control is concluded not effective for the year. How is it reported?

choices.label: Document it in the workpapers, evaluate the deficiency with the engagement team, tell them which automated controls and reports are affected, discuss it with management and include a recommendation in the management letter
choices.feedback: The financial audit team can then adapt its approach, for example with more substantive testing.

choices.label: Keep it within the IT audit team and only mention it orally to the IT manager
choices.feedback: The engagement team must know, because its reliance on the system changes.

exercises.answer: Investigate before concluding, never let evidence be created after the fact, assess the root cause and extent (shared privileged account, compensating controls), then rate and report the deficiency so the audit approach and the client’s remediation follow.

exercises.q: The audit team relies on SAP’s automated three-way match. The program-change ITGC for SAP were found not effective for the year. What follows?
options: Nothing: ITGC and application controls are tested separately
The auditors cannot simply rely on a test of one for the automated control: they test it more extensively, look for compensating controls or reduce reliance and do more substantive testing
The audit opinion on the accounts must be qualified
The client must redo all its changes of the year
exercises.answer: Without effective change control, nothing shows the program worked the same way all year, so a test of one is not enough. The auditors adapt the approach; an ITGC deficiency does not by itself change the opinion on the accounts.

interview.q: What is the difference between ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27002?
interview.a: ISO/IEC 27001 sets the requirements for an ISMS, clauses 4 to 10 plus the Annex A list of 93 controls, and is the one you certify against. ISO/IEC 27002 gives guidance on how to implement each of those controls, with attributes to filter them; nobody is certified to 27002. In practice 27001 says what must be in place, 27002 helps decide how.

interview.q: Can you exclude controls or clauses from the scope of certification?
interview.a: Clauses 4 to 10 cannot be excluded: they are the management system. Annex A controls can be excluded in the Statement of Applicability if the risk assessment and the scope justify it, for example physical data centre controls when everything is hosted at a cloud provider, whose controls are then covered through supplier management. The justification must be factual and consistent with the risk register.

interview.q: What does a Statement of Applicability contain and why do auditors care?
interview.a: For each necessary control and every Annex A control: whether it is included and why (risk, law, contract), whether it is implemented, and the justification for any exclusion. I also add owner, status and where the evidence is. Auditors use it as the map of the ISMS: they check it against the risk treatment plan and then sample controls marked implemented to see the evidence.

interview.q: How do you test whether a control operates effectively?
interview.a: First I check the design with a walkthrough. Then I get the complete population from the system for the period, with how it was extracted, pick a sample sized for the control frequency, and inspect or reperform each item. Inquiry alone does not count. Any exception is analysed: isolated or systemic, with the root cause, and the sample can be extended.

interview.q: What is the difference between a major and a minor nonconformity, and what happens after each?
interview.a: A major is the absence or total breakdown of a requirement, or a failure that puts the ISMS outcomes in doubt, such as no internal audit or no risk assessment. A minor is an isolated lapse. In a certification audit, majors must be corrected with evidence before the certificate is issued; minors need an accepted corrective action plan, verified at the next audit. In both cases I want a correction, a root cause and a corrective action with an effectiveness check.

interview.q: Walk me through an ISO 27001 certification cycle.
interview.a: Before the audit: gap analysis, risk assessment, SoA and treatment plan, controls running long enough to have records, one internal audit and a management review. Stage 1 reviews documentation and readiness; stage 2 tests implementation and effectiveness. Majors closed, the certification body decides and issues a three-year certificate. Surveillance audits in years one and two, then recertification. I would choose an accredited body, COFRAC-accredited in France, so the certificate is accepted by clients.

interview.q: A US prospect asks if you are SOC 2 compliant. You are ISO 27001 certified. What do you answer?
interview.a: I explain that we hold an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate, give its scope and offer the SoA under NDA, and that SOC 2 is a different deliverable: an AICPA attestation by a CPA firm on the Trust Services Criteria, Type II over a period. Many controls overlap, so if the market needs it we can map our control library to the SOC 2 criteria and plan a readiness assessment, then a Type I or directly a Type II period. Meanwhile, the certificate and a completed questionnaire often unblock the deal.

interview.q: How would you avoid audit fatigue when the company needs ISO 27001, SOC 2 and PCI DSS?
interview.a: One control library with owners, each control mapped once to every framework requirement, and one evidence calendar: evidence collected continuously, stored once and reused by each auditor. Internal audits test the shared controls, and audits are scheduled so the same samples can serve several of them where auditors accept it. A GRC tool helps, but the mapping and ownership are the real work.

interview.q: What are IT general controls, and why does a financial statement auditor care about them?
interview.a: ITGC are the controls over the systems that produce the accounts: access to programs and data, program changes, program development and computer operations. The auditors rely on automated controls and system reports; ITGC give assurance that programs and data could not be changed without control during the year, so those automated controls and reports behaved consistently. If ITGC fail, the audit team must test more, find compensating controls or move to substantive testing.

interview.q: A finance control uses a system report. How do you check you can rely on the report?
interview.a: I test it as IPE: completeness and accuracy. I understand how it is produced (standard or custom report, query and parameters), check the parameters used for the period, reconcile its total to the general ledger or another known figure, and trace a few lines from the report to the source and from the source to the report. If it is a custom report, I also check that changes to it fall under the change management ITGC. I keep the evidence of the run date and parameters.
